summary: Describes the OSPFv3 extensions required for Segment Routing with the MPLS data plane. It lets OSPFv3 routers advertise segments so end-to-end paths can be built from subpaths.

plainLanguage.summary: This is the same idea as the OSPFv2 version but for the map-sharing protocol used with IPv6, adding signposts so paths can be built from pieces.

questions: what is segment routing in ospfv3
subtitle: How OSPFv3 routers advertise Segment Routing identifiers so IPv6 networks can steer MPLS traffic along paths built from segments.

tldr.problem: Segment Routing encodes an end-to-end path as a sequence of segments, and the link-state routing protocols must advertise those segments. OSPFv3 had no way to carry them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a Prefix-SID sub-TLV, Adj-SID and LAN Adj-SID sub-TLVs, an SID/Label sub-TLV and an Extended Prefix Range TLV, plus rules for flooding them within an area, between areas and for external prefixes.
tldr.outcome: OSPFv3 can now program the MPLS data plane with Segment Routing, with no LDP or RSVP-TE signaling needed. The IPv6 data plane is out of scope and left to a separate document.

today: RFC 8666 is a Proposed Standard and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it. It covers only the MPLS data plane, and works together with RFC 8665, which specifies the OSPF capability advertisements.

sections.title: Segment Routing in OSPFv3
sections.content:
Segment Routing (SR) lets a network define flexible end-to-end paths inside an IGP topology by encoding a path as a sequence of topological subpaths called segments. The link-state protocols IS-IS and OSPF advertise these segments. A prefix segment stands for an ECMP-aware shortest path to a prefix or node, and is typically a multi-hop path. An adjacency segment stands for a hop over a specific adjacency between two nodes and is, in most cases, a one-hop path.

The SR control plane can be applied to both IPv6 and MPLS data planes, and it needs no extra signaling beyond the IGP extensions. In MPLS networks, SR paths need no LDP or RSVP-TE signaling, although SR can interoperate with LSPs set up by LDP or RSVP. This RFC covers only the MPLS data plane; the OSPFv3 extension for the IPv6 data plane is left to a separate document. The architecture itself is in RFC 8402.
sections.plainLanguage: A path is built from pieces: some pieces are long stretches to a faraway place, and some are a single step to the next neighbor. Routers announce the names of these pieces so anyone can chain them together.

sections.title: Segment Identifiers and Capabilities
sections.content:
Segment Routing defines several kinds of Segment Identifiers (SIDs): the Prefix-SID, the Adjacency SID and the LAN Adjacency SID. Whenever one of them is advertised, the actual SID or label is carried in a SID/Label sub-TLV, which has Type 7. Its Length is 3 or 4 octets. With length 3, the 20 rightmost bits are an MPLS label; with length 4, the value is a 32-bit SID.

SR also needs some router capabilities to be advertised to the other routers in the area. These go in the OSPFv3 Router Information Opaque LSA (from RFC 7770) and are specified in RFC 8665, not here.
sections.plainLanguage: Each road sign has a number on it. The number can be a small label or a bigger identifier, and the sign says which kind it is.

sections.title: The Extended Prefix Range TLV
sections.content:
Sometimes it helps to advertise attributes for a whole range of prefixes in one message. A Segment Routing Mapping Server (RFC 8661) is an example, since it advertises SIDs for many prefixes. The OSPFv3 Extended Prefix Range TLV (Type 9) handles contiguous prefixes of the same length. It is a top-level TLV of the E-Intra-Area-Prefix-LSA, E-Inter-Area-Prefix-LSA, E-AS-External-LSA and E-Type-7-LSA defined in RFC 8362, and several may appear in each LSA.

Its fields are Prefix Length, AF (0 for IPv4 unicast, 1 for IPv6 unicast), Range Size, Flags, a reserved field, the Address Prefix and optional sub-TLVs. The range starts at the given prefix, and the number of prefixes equals the Range Size. The Range Size MUST NOT exceed what the Prefix Length allows without including IPv4 multicast addresses (224.0.0.0/3) or, for IPv6, anything other than unicast addresses.

If the same range appears in several LSAs of the same type from the same router, the LSA with the numerically smallest Instance ID is used and the others MUST be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of writing one sign for each house on a street, you write one sign that says "starting at this house, the next seven houses". It saves a lot of writing.

sections.title: The Prefix-SID Sub-TLV
sections.content:
The Prefix-SID sub-TLV (Type 4) attaches a segment to a prefix. It is a sub-TLV of the Intra-Area Prefix, Inter-Area Prefix, External Prefix and Extended Prefix Range TLVs, and may appear more than once in its parent. Its Length is 7 or 8 octets depending on the V-Flag. After the flags come an Algorithm octet, a reserved field and the SID/Index/Label value.

The flags are NP (no penultimate hop popping), M (advertised by a Mapping Server), E (explicit null), V (value or index) and L (local or global). The V and L flags must be set together or clear together: both 0 means a 4-octet index into the SID/label space advertised by the router, and both 1 means a 3-octet local label. Any other combination is invalid and the advertisement MUST be ignored. A router that receives a Prefix-SID whose algorithm the remote node has not advertised in the SR-Algorithm TLV MUST ignore it, and if a router advertises several Prefix-SIDs for the same prefix, topology and algorithm, all of them MUST be ignored.

The NP and E flags control what upstream neighbors do with the label:

  • NP clear: the upstream neighbor MUST pop the Prefix-SID, like penultimate hop popping in MPLS. The E flag is ignored.
  • NP set and E clear: the neighbor MUST keep the Prefix-SID on top of the stack. This suits an ABR or ASBR that stitches the packet into a continuing LSP.
  • NP and E both set: the neighbor MUST replace the Prefix-SID with an Explicit NULL label (0 for IPv4, 2 for IPv6).

NP MUST be set and E MUST be clear for Prefix-SIDs of prefixes propagated between areas by an ABR, or redistributed by an ASBR, unless the prefix is directly attached to that router. When M is set, NP and E MUST be ignored on reception.
sections.plainLanguage: A prefix sign says which place it points to and how to treat the sign when you get near. Either take it off one step early, leave it on, or swap it for a plain sign.

sections.title: Adjacency Segments
sections.content:
An Adj-SID identifies a router's adjacency. The Adj-SID sub-TLV (Type 5) is an optional sub-TLV of the Router-Link TLV and may appear several times. Its flags are B (backup: the adjacency is eligible for protection such as IP or MPLS fast reroute), V, L, G (group: the Adj-SID refers to a group of adjacencies) and P (persistent: the value stays the same across router restart or interface flap). A Weight field is used for load balancing, as defined in RFC 8402.

A router MAY allocate an Adj-SID to each adjacency, MAY allocate more than one to an adjacency, and MAY give the same Adj-SID to different adjacencies. When P is set, the Adj-SID MUST be persistent.

The LAN Adj-SID sub-TLV (Type 6) is for adjacencies to non-DR routers on broadcast, NBMA or hybrid networks. It adds a Neighbor ID field holding the Router ID of the neighbor, and its Length is 11 or 12 octets.
sections.plainLanguage: An adjacency sign points at one specific neighbor, like "take the door to the next room". On a busy shared hallway, the sign also names which neighbor it means.

sections.title: Procedures Within and Between Areas
sections.content:
Inside an area, an SR-capable OSPFv3 router MAY advertise Prefix-SIDs for any prefix it advertises reachability to, such as a loopback address. A Mapping Server can advertise Prefix-SIDs for remote prefixes; several Mapping Servers advertising the same prefix MUST advertise the same Prefix-SID. A Mapping Server MUST use Extended Prefix Range TLVs, with an E-Intra-Area-Prefix-LSA for area flooding scope or an E-AS-External-LSA for AS flooding scope. It MUST set the NU-bit in PrefixOptions so the advertisement does not itself create prefix reachability.

Across areas, OSPFv3 MUST propagate Prefix-SID information. When an ABR advertises an Inter-Area-Prefix-LSA, it includes a Prefix-SID sub-TLV taken from the router on its best path to the prefix. If that router advertised none, the ABR uses a Prefix-SID advertised by any other router.

For external prefixes, an ASBR that originates an E-AS-External-LSA SHOULD include a Prefix-SID sub-TLV. An NSSA ABR translating an E-NSSA-LSA into an E-AS-External-LSA SHOULD also advertise the Prefix-SID, following the same best-path rule.

Adj-SIDs on point-to-point links MAY be advertised for neighbors in state 2-Way or higher, and MUST be withdrawn if the adjacency drops below 2-Way. On broadcast, NBMA or hybrid networks, routers advertise an Adj-SID for the adjacency to the DR with the Adj-SID sub-TLV, and MAY advertise LAN Adj-SIDs for other neighbors such as the BDR or DR-OTHER routers.
sections.plainLanguage: Signs are posted in the home town. When a sign is passed to the next town, the border guard copies the sign from whoever knows the best way, so people there can use it too.

sections.title: Error Handling and IANA Registrations
sections.content:
For any new TLV or sub-TLV, if the length is invalid, the LSA carrying it is considered malformed and MUST be ignored. Errors SHOULD be logged, subject to rate limiting.

The RFC updates two OSPFv3 registries: the Extended-LSA TLVs registry gets value 9 (OSPFv3 Extended Prefix Range TLV), and the Extended-LSA Sub-TLVs registry gets 4 (Prefix-SID), 5 (Adj-SID), 6 (LAN Adj-SID) and 7 (SID/Label).
sections.plainLanguage: If a sign is the wrong size, it is thrown away, and the problem is written down, but not too often. The new sign kinds get official numbers in a master list.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
With these extensions OSPFv3 programs the MPLS data plane. Previously LDP or another label distribution mechanism was required to advertise MPLS labels. The same types of attacks possible on the IP control plane are possible on the MPLS control plane and can misroute traffic, though the latter can be harder to detect and isolate.

The existing OSPFv3 security extensions from RFC 5340 and RFC 8362 apply. Where attackers might have access to the routing domain, stronger authentication such as that in RFC 4552 or RFC 7166 SHOULD be used. Implementations MUST ensure malformed TLVs and sub-TLVs cannot crash the router or routing process, and logging of them SHOULD be rate limited to avoid a denial-of-service attack on the control plane.
sections.plainLanguage: Because routers now hand out the road signs themselves, a bad guy who tricks them could send traffic the wrong way. So the routers should check who is talking, and not fall over when they see a broken sign.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: 7 or 8 octets, depending on the V-Flag.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: NP, M, E, V and L flags.

fields.name: Algorithm
fields.desc: Algorithm the Prefix-SID is associated with.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Set to 0 on transmission, ignored on reception.

fields.name: SID/Index/Label
fields.desc: Variable: a 4-octet index or a 3-octet local label.

items.label: No-PHP
items.desc: If set, the penultimate hop MUST NOT pop the Prefix-SID.

items.label: Mapping Server
items.desc: The SID was advertised by an SR Mapping Server.

items.label: Explicit Null
items.desc: Upstream neighbor replaces the Prefix-SID with Explicit NULL.

items.label: Value/Index
items.desc: Set: absolute value. Clear: an index.

items.label: Local/Global
items.desc: Set: local significance. Clear: global significance.
